---
title: "Independence"
---

Suppose that we learn a pronoun is plural. Does that information change how likely the pronoun is to have accusative form? Conditional probability lets us state the question precisely:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\stackrel{?}{=}\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

In the toy pronoun measure,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70
$$

but

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
$$

Restricting attention to plural forms changes the probability of accusative form. The two events are associated under this measure.

Events $B$ and $C$ are [**independent**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) when

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

This definition compares the observed mass in the intersection with the mass that would result from multiplying the two margins.

## Check the pronoun events by hand

The marginal probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)=.50
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70.
$$

Their product is

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)\mathbb{P}(A)
=.50\times.70
=.35.
$$

The observed joint probability is

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40.
$$

Since $.40\neq.35$, the events are not independent under this measure.

The same conclusion follows from conditioning. The probability of $A$ changes from $.70$ in the full space to $.80$ within $P$.

## Connect the two statements

When $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, the [product rule](probability-factorization.qmd) gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

If $B$ and $C$ are independent, the definition also gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

Equate the right sides and divide by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Thus independence has a conditional interpretation: learning that $C$ occurred does not change the probability of $B$.

## Build an independent comparison measure

Keep the same outcome labels and margins, but change how the mass is arranged inside the table.

| | accusative $A$ | nominative $A^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plural $P$ | $.35$ | $.15$ | $.50$ |
| singular $P^c$ | $.35$ | $.15$ | $.50$ |
| total | $.70$ | $.30$ | $1$ |

Now the upper left cell equals the product of its margins:

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
=.35
=.50\times.70.
$$

Conditioning gives the same result:

$$
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{.35}{.50}
=.70
=\mathbb{P}(A).
$$

The accusative proportion is also $.70$ in the singular row. Knowing the number category provides no information about case under this new measure.

```{r}
#| eval: false
joint_independent <- matrix(
  c(.35, .35, .15, .15),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

p_joint <- joint_independent["plural", "accusative"]
p_plural <- sum(joint_independent["plural", ])
p_acc <- sum(joint_independent[, "accusative"])

c(observed = p_joint, product = p_plural * p_acc)
```

Both returned values are `.35`.

## Independence belongs to the measure

The two tables use the same outcome labels and the same events. The original table makes $P$ and $A$ dependent; the comparison table makes them independent. Independence is thus a property of events under a probability measure, not a property of the linguistic labels alone.

This matters when interpreting corpus data. A construction choice and an animacy feature may appear independent in one genre but associated in another. The sample space may represent the same categories in both cases, while the probability measure changes with the population of tokens.

## Independence is not mutual exclusivity

Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. If two mutually exclusive events $B$ and $C$ both have positive probability, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)=0
$$

while

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)>0.
$$

They are not independent. Observing $C$ tells us that $B$ did not occur, which is strong information.

Mutual exclusivity concerns whether the intersection is empty. Independence concerns whether the intersection receives the product of the marginal probabilities.

## A common failure: no difference means independence

A small difference in a finite sample does not establish independence. Independence is an exact claim about a probability measure. Estimated proportions from finite data will rarely match exactly, even when an independence model is useful, and they may match by chance when the underlying events are associated.

Later chapters introduce statistical models for uncertainty about such claims. At this stage, we can determine only whether a fully specified probability measure satisfies the independence equation.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify independence in the comparison table using both the product definition and the conditional interpretation.
2. Change the upper left cell from $.35$ to $.40$ and the lower left cell from $.35$ to $.30$, leaving the margins fixed. Does independence still hold?
3. Explain why two mutually exclusive events with positive probability cannot be independent.
4. Give a linguistic setting in which the same two event labels might be independent in one represented population but dependent in another.

This completes the foundations sequence. We have built probability claims from represented outcomes, measurable events, and a coherent measure. Continue to the [next module](../random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd) when you are ready to add the next object in the dependency sequence.
